entries.08b06c97a990482b55dc258c39d2029318d0c30c: <div sID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="146" osisID="Ps.146" sID="Ps.146"/> <div eID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> This and all the rest of the psalms that follow begin and end with Hallelujah, a word which puts much of God's praise into a little compass; for in it we praise him by his name Jah, the contraction of Jehovah. In this excellent psalm of praise, I. The psalmist engages himself to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1-Ps.146.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He engages others to trust in him, which is one necessary and acceptable way of praising him. 1. He shows why we should not trust in men, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3-Ps.146.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. 2. Why we should trust in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">ver. 5</reference>), because of his power in the kingdom of nature (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.6">ver. 6</reference>), his dominion in the kingdom of providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.7">ver. 7</reference>), and his grace in the kingdom of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.8-Ps.146.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), that everlasting kingdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.10">ver. 10</reference>), to which many of the Jewish writers refer this psalm, and to which therefore we should have an eye, in the singing of it.
entries.6ef683de0572d8ca37c59b8f121c4b52772b6c20: <div eID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Bounty.</title> <div sID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul. <hi type="super">2</hi> While I live will I praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being. <hi type="super">3</hi> Put not your trust in princes, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> in the son of man, in whom <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no help. <hi type="super">4</hi> His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish. <div eID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> David is supposed to have penned this psalm; and he was himself a prince, a mighty prince; as such, it might be thought, 1. That he should be exempted from the service of praising God, that it was enough for him to see that his priests and people did it, but that he needed not to do it himself in his own person. Michal thought it a disparagement to him to <hi type="italic">dance before the ark;</hi> but he was so far from being of this mind that he would himself be first and foremost in the work, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1-Ps.146.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. He considered his dignity as so far from excusing him from it that it rather obliged him to lead in it, and he thought it so far from lessening him that it really magnified him; therefore he stirred up himself to it and to make a business of it: <hi type="italic">Praise the Lord, O my soul!</hi> and he resolved to abide by it: "I will praise him with my heart, <hi type="italic">I will sing praises</hi> to him with my mouth. Herein I will have an eye to him as <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> infinitely blessed and glorious in himself, and as <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> in covenant with me." Praise is most pleasant when, in praising God, we have an eye to him as ours, whom we have an interest in and stand in relation to. "This I will do constantly while I live, every day of my life, and to my life's end; nay, I will do it <hi type="italic">while I have any being,</hi> for when I have no being on earth I hope to have a being in heaven, a better being, to be doing it better." That which is the great end of our being ought to be our great employment and delight while we have any being. "In thee must our time and powers be spent." 2. It might be thought that he himself, having been so great a blessing to his country, should be adored, according to the usage of the heathen nations, who deified their heroes, that they should all come and <hi type="italic">trust in his shadow</hi> and make him their <hi type="italic">stay</hi> and <hi type="italic">strong-hold.</hi> "No," says David, "<hi type="italic">Put not your trust in princes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">v. 3</reference>), not in me, not in any other; do not repose your confidence in them; do not raise your expectations from them. Be not too sure of their sincerity; some have thought they knew better how to reign by knowing how to dissemble. Be not too sure of their constancy and fidelity; it is possible they may both change their minds and break their words." But, though we suppose them very wise and as good as David himself, yet we must not be too sure of their ability and continuance, for they are sons of Adam, weak and mortal. There is indeed a Son of man in whom there is help, in whom there is salvation, and who will not fail those that trust in him. But all other sons of men are like the man they are sprung of, who, being in honour, did not abide. (1.) We cannot be sure of their ability. Even the power of kings may be so straitened, cramped, and weakened, that they may not be in a capacity to do that for us which we expect. David himself owned (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.39">2 Sam. iii. 39</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am this day weak, though anointed king.</hi> So that <hi type="italic">in the son of man there is</hi> often <hi type="italic">no help,</hi> no salvation; he is at a loss, at his wits' end, as <hi type="italic">a man astonished,</hi> and then, though <hi type="italic">a mighty man,</hi> he <hi type="italic">cannot save,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer. xiv. 9</reference>. (2.) We cannot be sure of their continuance. Suppose he has it in his power to help us while he lives, yet he may be suddenly taken off when we expect most from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">His breath goes forth,</hi> so it does every moment, and comes back again, but that is an intimation that it will shortly go for good and all, and then <hi type="italic">he returns to his earth.</hi> The earth is his, in respect of his original as a man, the earth out of which he was taken, and to which therefore he must return, according to the sentence, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen. iii. 19</reference>. It is his, if he be a worldly man, in respect of choice, his earth which he has chosen for his portion, and on the things of which he has set his affections. He shall go to his own place. Or, rather, it is his earth because of the property he has in it; and though he has had large possessions on earth a grave is all that will remain to him. <hi type="italic">The earth God has given to the children of men,</hi> and great striving there is about it, and, as a mark of their authority, men <hi type="italic">call their lands by their own names.</hi> But, after a while, no part of the earth will be their own but that in which the dead body shall make its bed, and that shall be theirs <hi type="italic">while the earth remains.</hi> But, when he returns to his earth, <hi type="italic">in that very day his thoughts perish;</hi> all the projects and designs he had of kindness to us vanish and are gone, and he cannot take one step further in them; all his purposes are cut off and buried with him, <reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job xvii. 11</reference>. And then what becomes of our expectations from him? Princes are mortal, as well as other men, and therefore we cannot have that assurance of help from them which we may have from that Potentate who hath immortality. <hi type="italic">Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils</hi> and will not be there long.
entries.ad6c87a8bf0e42fac6b6956217dfa73340ae4f5b: <div eID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Trust in God.</title> <div sID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">is he</hi> that <hi type="italic">hath</hi> the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God: <hi type="super">6</hi> Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein <hi type="italic">is:</hi> which keepeth truth for ever: <hi type="super">7</hi> Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> looseth the prisoners: <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> openeth <hi type="italic">the eyes of</hi> the blind: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> raiseth them that are bowed down: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> loveth the righteous: 9 The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he turneth upside down. <hi type="super">10</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall reign for ever, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thy God, O Zion, unto all generations. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having cautioned us not to trust in princes (because, if we do, we shall be miserably disappointed), here encourages us to put our confidence in God, because, if we do so, we shall be happily secured: <hi type="italic">Happy is he that has the God of Jacob for his help,</hi> that has an interest in his attributes and promises, and has them engaged for him, and <hi type="italic">whose hope is in the Lord his God.</hi> <div eID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> I. Let us take a view of the character here given of those whom God will uphold. Those shall have God for their help, 1. Who take him for their God, and serve and worship him accordingly. 2. Who have their hope in him, and live a life of dependence upon him, who have good thoughts of him, and encourage themselves in him, when all other supports fail. Every believer may look upon him as the God of Jacob, of the church in general, and therefore may expect relief from him, in reference to public distresses, and as his God in particular, and therefore may depend upon him in all personal wants and straits. We must hope, (1.) In the providence of God for all the good things we need, which relate to the life that now is. (2.) In the grace of Christ for all the good things which relate to the life that is to come. To this especially the learned Dr. Hammond refers this and the following verses, looking upon the latter part of this psalm to have a most visible remarkable aspect towards the eternal Son of God in his incarnation. He quotes one of the rabbies, who says of <reference osisRef="Ps.146.10">v. 10</reference> that it belongs to the days of the Messiah. And that it does so he thinks will appear by comparing <reference osisRef="Ps.146.7-Ps.146.8">v. 7, 8</reference>, with the characters Christ gives of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.5-Matt.11.6">Matt. xi. 5, 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">The blind receive their sight, the lame walk;</hi> and the closing words there, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he whosoever shall not be offended in me,</hi> he thinks may very well be supposed to refer to <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that hopes in the Lord his God,</hi> and who is not offended in him. <div eID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13258" type="x-p"/> II. Let us take a view of the great encouragements here given us to hope in <hi type="italic">the Lord our God.</hi> 1. He is the <hi type="italic">Maker of the world,</hi> and therefore has all power in himself, and the command of the powers of all the creatures, which, being derived from him, depend upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is,</hi> and therefore his arm is not shortened, that it cannot save. It is very applicable to Christ, by whom God made the world, and <hi type="italic">without whom was not any thing made that was made.</hi> It is a great support to faith that the Redeemer of the world is the same that was the Creator of it, and therefore has a good-will to it, a perfect knowledge of its case, and power to help it. 2. He is a God of inviolable fidelity. We may venture to take God's word, for he <hi type="italic">keepeth truth for ever,</hi> and therefore no word of his shall fall to the ground; it is true <hi type="italic">from the beginning,</hi> and therefore true <hi type="italic">to the end.</hi> Our Lord Jesus is the Amen, <hi type="italic">the faithful witness,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">the beginning,</hi> the author and principle, <hi type="italic">of the creation of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev. iii. 14</reference>. The keeping of God's truth for ever is committed to him, for <hi type="italic">all the promises</hi> are in him <hi type="italic">yea and amen.</hi> 3. He is the patron of injured innocency: <hi type="italic">He pleads the cause of the oppressed,</hi> and (as we read it) he <hi type="italic">executes judgment</hi> for them. He often does it in his providence, giving redress to those that suffer wrong and clearing up their integrity. He will do it in the judgment of the great day. The Messiah came to rescue the children of men out of the hands of Satan the great oppressor, and, all judgment being committed to him, the executing of judgment upon persecutors is so among the rest, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. 4. He is a bountiful benefactor to the necessitous: <hi type="italic">He gives food to the hungry;</hi> so God does in an ordinary way for the answering of the cravings of nature; so he has done sometimes in an extraordinary way, as when ravens fed Elijah; so Christ did more than once when he fed thousands miraculously with that which was intended but for one meal or two for his own family. This encourages us to hope in him as the nourisher of our souls with the bread of life. 5. He is the author of liberty to those that were bound: <hi type="italic">The Lord looseth the prisoners.</hi> He brought Israel out of the house of bondage in Egypt and afterwards in Babylon. The miracles Christ wrought, in making the dumb to speak and the deaf to hear with that one word, <hi type="italic">Ephphatha—Be opened,</hi> his cleansing lepers, and so discharging them from their confinements, and his raising the dead out of their graves, may all be included in this one of <hi type="italic">loosing the prisoners;</hi> and we may take encouragement from those to hope in him for that spiritual liberty which he came to proclaim, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.2">Isa. lxi. 1, 2</reference>. 6. He gives sight to those that have been long deprived of it; <hi type="italic">The Lord can open the eyes of the blind,</hi> and has often given to his afflicted people to see that comfort which before they were not aware of; witness <reference osisRef="Gen.21.19">Gen. xxi. 19</reference>, and the prophet's servant, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings vi. 17</reference>. But this has special reference to Christ; for <hi type="italic">since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind</hi> till Christ did it (<reference osisRef="John.9.32">John ix. 32</reference>) and thereby encouraged us to hope in him for spiritual illumination. 7. He sets that straight which was crooked, and makes those easy that were pained and ready to sink: He <hi type="italic">raises those that are bowed down,</hi> by comforting and supporting them under their burdens, and, in due time, removing their burdens. This was literally performed by Christ when he made a poor woman straight that had been <hi type="italic">bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.12">Luke xiii. 12</reference>); and he still does it by his grace, giving rest to those that were weary and heavily laden, and raising up with his comforts those that were humbled and cast down by convictions. 8. He has a constant kindness for all good people: <hi type="italic">The Lord loveth the righteous,</hi> and they may with the more confidence depend upon his power when they are sure of his good-will. Our Lord Jesus showed his love to the righteous <hi type="italic">by fulfilling all righteousness.</hi> 9. He has a tender concern for those that stand in special need of his care: <hi type="italic">The Lord preserves the strangers.</hi> It ought not to pass without remark that the name of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> is repeated here five times in five lines, to intimate that it is an almighty power (that of Jehovah) that is engaged and exerted for the relief of the oppressed, and that it is as much the glory of God to succour those that are in misery as it is to <hi type="italic">ride on the heavens by his name Jah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.4">Ps. lxviii. 4</reference>. (1.) Strangers are exposed, and are commonly destitute of friends, but <hi type="italic">the Lord preserves them,</hi> that they be not run down and ruined. Many a poor stranger has found the benefit of the divine protection and been kept alive by it. (2.) <hi type="italic">Widows and fatherless children,</hi> that have lost the head of the family, who took care of the affairs of it, often fall into the hands of those that make a prey of them, that will not do them justice, nay, that will do them injustice; but <hi type="italic">the Lord relieveth them,</hi> and raiseth up friends for them. See <reference osisRef="Exod.22.22-Exod.22.23">Exod. xxii. 22, 23</reference>. Our Lord Jesus came into the world to help the helpless, to receive Gentiles, strangers, into his kingdom, and that with him poor sinners, that are as fatherless, <hi type="italic">may find mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">Hos. xiv. 3</reference>. 10. He will appear for the destruction of all those that oppose his kingdom and oppress the faithful subjects of it: <hi type="italic">The way of the wicked he turns upside down,</hi> and therefore let us <hi type="italic">hope in him,</hi> and not be <hi type="italic">afraid of the fury of the oppressor,</hi> as though he were <hi type="italic">ready to destroy.</hi> It is the glory of the Messiah that he will subvert all the counsels of hell and earth that militate against his church, so that, having him for us, we need not fear any thing that can be done against us. 11. His kingdom shall continue through all the revolutions of time, to the utmost ages of eternity, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.10">v. 10</reference>. Let <hi type="italic">this</hi> encourage us to trust in God at all times that <hi type="italic">the Lord shall reign for ever,</hi> in spite of all the malignity of the powers of darkness, <hi type="italic">even thy God, O Zion! unto all generations.</hi> Christ is set King on the holy hill of Zion, and his kingdom shall continue in an endless glory. It cannot be destroyed by an invader; it shall not be left to a successor, either to a succeeding monarch or a succeeding monarchy, but it shall stand for ever. It is matter of unspeakable comfort that <hi type="italic">the Lord reigns</hi> as Zion's God, as Zion's king, that the Messiah is head over all things to the church, and will be so while the world stands.  <chapter eID="Ps.146"/> <div eID="gen13258" type="x-p"/>

entries.75457024ae914bd8fd904d0a8dda4cb5a00fe4f8: <chapter n="146" osisID="Ps.146" sID="Ps.146"/><div eID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7129"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 146</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.146.1-Ps.146.10">Psa 146:1-10</reference>. An exhortation to praise God, who, by the gracious and faithful exercise of His power in goodness to the needy, is alone worthy of implicit trust.</title> <div sID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.146"/>

entries.de30a30ba4feff7eaf7c767672f1b0acce129fe8: <div eID="gen23518" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23520" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, full of gratitude, purposes to praise God for ever, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.1">Psa 146:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.2">Psa 146:2</reference>; and exhorts not to trust in man, not even the most powerful; for which he gives his reasons, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.3">Psa 146:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.4">Psa 146:4</reference>. The great advantage of trusting in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.5">Psa 146:5</reference>. The mercies which they who trust in God may expect, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.6-Psa.146.9">Psa 146:6-9</reference>. The Divine government is everlasting, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.10">Psa 146:10</reference>. <div eID="gen23520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23521" type="x-p"/> This is the first of the Psalms called Hallelujah Psalms, of which there are five, and which conclude the book. No author's name is prefixed to this, either in the Hebrew or Chaldee. But the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, attribute it to Haggai and Zechariah. It was probably written after the captivity, and may refer to the time when Cyrus, prejudiced by the enemies of the Jews, withdrew his order for the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, to which revocation of the royal edict the third verse may refer: Put not your trust in princes etc.
entries.d4ce7a2ed0f2d88d7e6dd154a3983204b8177a13: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> While I live will I praise - The true feeling of a heart overpowered with a sense of God's goodness. <div eID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> While I have any being - בעודי beodi, in my continuance, in my progression, my eternal existence. This is very expressive.
entries.71c84d8c82f3a4a04871772d007e55df6d9aa982: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> Put not your trust in princes - This may refer, as has been stated above, to Cyrus, who had revoked his edict for the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Perhaps they had begun to suppose that they were about to owe their deliverance to the Persian king. God permitted this change in the disposition of the king, to teach them the vanity of confidence in men, and the necessity of trusting in himself.
entries.174dea5ff33de7492b1dcfb863885a1bd2edb2e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> His breath goeth forth - His existence depends merely, under God, on the air he breathes. When he ceases to respire he ceases to live; his body from that moment begins to claim its affinity to the earth; and all his thoughts, purposes, and projects, whether good or evil, come to nought and perish. He, then, who has no other dependence, must necessarily be miserable.
entries.349ab98ef31703c3af9dfcabbc26f529ffc2f71d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23526" type="x-p"/> Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help - While he that trusts in man is miserable, he that trusts in God is happy. In the son of man, בן אדם ben Adam, there is no help, תשועה teshuah, no saving principle. Every son of Adam naturally comes into the world without this, and must continue so till the Lord open the eyes of the blind, <reference osisRef="Psa.146.8">Psa 146:8</reference>; but a measure of light is given from that true Light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. This son of Adam returns to his earth, לאדמתו leadmatho, to the ground, from which he was taken; this refers directly to <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen 3:19</reference>. But he that has the God for his help who helped Jacob in his distress, and was with him, and sustained him in and through all adversities, can never be destitute; for this God changes not; he lives for ever, and his projects cannot perish. He has purposed that Israel shall be delivered from this captivity. Cyrus may change, but God will not; trust therefore in Him. He has all power; he made heaven and earth; he has them under his government and at his disposal; and should earth itself fail, heaven endures. And he keeps his truth for ever; and therefore his promises must be fulfilled to them that trust in him. Fear not.
entries.1aefb873449111f2160a1eaea542b6f81bf80c75: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23527" type="x-p"/> Which ewecuteth judgment for the oppressed - For those who suffer by violence or calumny. This may refer to the Israelites, who suffered much by oppression from the Babylonians, and by calumny from the Samaritans, etc., who had prejudiced the king of Persia against them. <div eID="gen23527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23528" type="x-p"/> Giving food to the hungry - No doubt he fed the poor captives by many displays of his peculiar providence. <div eID="gen23528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> The Lord looseth the prisoners - And as he has sustained you so long under your captivity, so will he bring you out of it.
entries.3bfbcec3ad183f2ed09d63a71ff9795c78835569: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23530" type="x-p"/> Openeth the eyes of the blind - He brings us out of our prison-house, from the shadow of death, and opens our eyes that we may behold the free light of the day. And it is the Lord only that can open the eyes of any son of Adam, and give him to see his wretchedness, and where help and salvation may be found. <div eID="gen23530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23531" type="x-p"/> Raiseth them that are bowed down - Through a sense of their guilt and sinfulness. <div eID="gen23531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23532" type="x-p"/> The Lord loveth the righteous - These he makes partakers of a Divine nature; and he loves those who bear his own image.
entries.b805c20deccb1839f1c872efe1ec0503ac7950ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23533" type="x-p"/> Preserveth the strangers - He has preserved you strangers in a strange land, where you have been in captivity for seventy years; and though in an enemy's country, he has provided for the widows and orphans as amply as if he had been in the promised land. <div eID="gen23533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> The way of the wicked he turneth upside down - He subverts, turns aside. They shall not do all the wickedness they wish; they shall not do all that is in their power. In their career he will either stop them, turn them aside, or overturn them.
entries.703e4182500ac3fb2ddab2a504512c5a4b142070: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23535" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall reign for ever - Therefore he can never fail; and he is thy God, O Zion. Hitherto he has helped you and your fathers; and has extended that help from generation to generation. Therefore trust in him and bless the Lord.  <chapter eID="Ps.146"/> <div eID="gen23535" type="x-p"/>

entries.e0221f28c58787bf75f48a3c6351a4561ca2cb86: <div eID="gen10328" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hallelujah to God the One True Helper</title> <div sID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> The Psalter now draws to a close with five Hallelujah Psalms. This first closing Hallelujah has many points of coincidence with the foregoing alphabetical hymn (compare אחללה in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.2">Psa 146:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.2">Psa 145:2</reference>; שׂברו in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">Psa 146:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.15">Psa 145:15</reference>; “who giveth bread to the hungry” in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.7">Psa 146:7</reference> with Psa 145:15.; “who maketh the blind to see” in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.8">Psa 146:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.14">Psa 145:14</reference>; “Jahve reigneth, etc.,” in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.10">Psa 146:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">Psa 145:13</reference>) - the same range of thought betrays one author. In the lxx <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1">Psa 146:1</reference> (according to its enumeration four Psalms, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.145.1">Psa 145:1</reference>, Psalms 147 being split up into two) have the inscription Ἀλληλούια. Ἀγγαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου, which is repeated four times. These Psalms appear to have formed a separate Hallel, which is referred back to these prophets, in the old liturgy of the second Temple. Later on they became, together with <reference osisRef="Ps.149.1">Psa 149:1</reference>, an integral part of the daily morning prayer, and in fact of the פסוקי דזמרה, i.e., of the mosaic-work of Psalms and other poetical pieces that was incorporated in the morning prayer, and are called eve in <hi type="italic">Shabbath</hi> 118 <hi type="italic">b</hi> <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi>,<note placement="foot">Rashi, however, understands only <reference osisRef="Ps.148.1-Ps.148.14">Psa 148:1-14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.150.1-Ps.150.6">Psa 150:1-6</reference> by פסוקי דזמרה in that passage.</note> but expressly distinguished from the Hallel to be recited at the Passover and other feasts, which is called “the Egyptian Hallel.” In distinction from this, Krochmal calls these five Psalms the Greek Hallel. But there is nothing to oblige us to come down beyond the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. The agreement between 1 Macc. 2:63 (ἔστρεψεν εἰς τὸν χοῦν αὐτοῦ καὶ ὁ διαλογισμὸς αὐτοῦ ἀπώλετο) and <reference osisRef="Ps.146.4">Psa 146:4</reference> of our Psalm, which Hitzig has turned to good account, does not decide anything concerning the age of the Psalm, but only shows that it was in existence at the time of the author of the First Book of Maccabees, - a point in favour of which we were not in need of any proof. But there was just as much ground for dissuading against putting confidence in princes in the time of the Persians as in that of the Grecian domination.
entries.c943a5099ee4871a8aacd9a23aa49522de25f892: <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1-Ps.146.4">Psa 146:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10330" type="x-p"/> Instead of “bless,” as in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">Psa 103:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.1">Psa 104:1</reference>, the poet of this Psalm says “praise.” When he attunes his sole to the praise of God, he puts himself personally into this mood of mind, and therefore goes on to say “I will praise.” He will, however, not only praise God in the song which he is beginning, but כּחיּי (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>), fillling up his life with it, or בּעודי (prop. “in my yet-being,” with the suffix of the noun, whereas עודנּי with the verbal suffix is “I still am”), so that his continued life is also a constant continued praising, viz., (and this is in the mind of the poet here, even at the commencment of the Psalm) of the God and Kings who, as being the Almighty, Eternal, and unchangeably Faithful One, is the true ground of confidence. The warning against putting trust in princes calls to mind Psa 118:8. The clause: the son of man, who has no help that he could afford, is to be understood according to Ps 60:13. The following לאדמתו shows that the poet by expression בּן־אדם combines the thoughts of <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference> and Gen 3:19. If his breath goes forth, he says, basing the untrustworthiness and feebleness of the son of Adam upon the inevitable final destiny of the son of Adam taken out of the ground, then he returns to his earth, i.e., the earth of his first beginning; cf. the more exact expression אל־עפרם, after which the εἰς τὴν γῆν αὐτοῦ of the lxx is exchanged for εἰς τὸν χοῦν αὐτοῦ in 1 Macc. 2:63: On the hypothetical relation of the first future clause to the second, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8-Ps.139.10">Psa 139:8-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.18">Psa 139:18</reference>; Ew. §357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. In that day, the inevitable day of death, the projects or plans of man are at once and forever at an end. The ἅπ. λεγ. עשׁתּנת describes these with the collateral notion of the subtleness and magnitude.
entries.875008864bc6cb11f5f032add6ce0881cd4da8e4: <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5-Ps.146.7">Psa 146:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen10330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10331" type="x-p"/> Man’s help is of no avail; blessed is he (this is the last of the twenty-five אשׁרי of the Psalter), on the contrary, who has the God of Jacob (שׁאל like שׁיהוה in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">Psa 144:15</reference>) as Him in whom is his succour (בּעזרו with <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.35.2">Psa 35:2</reference>) - he, whose confidence (שׂבר as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.116">Psa 119:116</reference>) rests on Jahve, whom he can by faith call his God. Men often are not able to give help although they might be willing to do so: He, however, is the Almighty, the Creator of the heavens, the earth, and the sea, and of all living things that fill these three (cf. <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Neh 9:6</reference>). Men easily change their mind and do not keep their word: He, however, is He who keepeth truth or faithfulness, inasmuch as He unchangeably adheres to the fulfilling of His promises. שׁמר אמת is in form equivalent substantially to שׁמר חסד and שׁמר הבּרית. And that which He is able to do as being the Almighty, and cannot as being the Truthful One leave undone, is also really His mode of active manifestation made evident in practical proofs: He obtains right for the oppressed, gives bread to the hungry, and consequently proves Himself to be the succour of those who suffer wrong without doing wrong, and as the provider for those who look for their daily bread from His gracious hand. With השּׁמר, the only determinate participle, the faithfulness of God to His promises is made especially prominent.

entries.ed71d69b3ce23337f9c5056bd5d052e35ff0e377:
PSALM 146
In the original Hebrew and in the Chaldee paraphrase, no author’s name is prefixed to this Psalm: in the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, AEthiopic, and Arabic versions it is ascribed to Haggai and Zechariah. Upon the supposition that it was written by these Prophets its composition would be after the captivity; “and it may refer,” says Dr. Adam Clarke, “to the time when Cyrus, prejudiced by the enemies of the Jews, withdrew his order for the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, to which revocation of the royal edict the Psalm 146:3 may refer, ‘Put not your trust in princes,’ etc.” Horsley, proceeding on the same view, entitles it, “A thanksgiving of the returning captives.” There is, however, nothing in it which prohibits us from looking upon it as a Psalm of David.
After stirring up himself, and others by his example, to praise God, David animadverts upon the diseased disposition, almost universally prevalent, to deceive ourselves by expectations entertained from various quarters. He, at the same time, points out the remedy — that our whole hope should be centered in God. To persuade us to resort to him more readily, he touches shortly upon some proofs of his power and mercy.
Hallelujah.
Psalm 146:1-5
1. Praise Jehovah, O my soul! 2. I will praise Jehovah in my life; I will sing psalms to my God so long as I shall have being. 3. Trust not in princes; in the son of man in whom there is not safety. 4. His breath shall go forth; he shall return to his earth, in that day his thoughts
Horsley prefers translating “his false deceitful show,” instead of “his thoughts.” He observes, that the original word is literally “his glitterings.” Parkhurst would render the original word “splendours, glories,” “which,” says he, “makes an excellent sense.”
shall perish. 5. Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in Jehovah, his God.
 
1. Praise Jehovah. The five last Psalms close with the same word with which they begin.
That is, with the word “Hallelujah,” the Hebrew for “Praise Jehovah.” Hence they have been called, “Hallelujah Psalms.”
But having in general called upon all to praise God, he addresses himself, or, which is the same thing, his soul, only that under the name of soul he addresses his inward self more emphatically. We may infer from this, that the influence which moved him was not volatile and superficial, (as many will blame themselves with remissness on this point, and then immediately lapse into it again,) but a staid and constant affection, followed up by activity, and proved by its effects not to be feigned. As David felt, that good endeavors are frustrated or hindered through the craft of Satan, he thinks it proper to apply a stimulus for exciting his own zeal, in the first place, before professing to be a leader or teacher to others. Although his heart was truly and seriously in the work, he would not rest in this, until he had acquired still greater ardor. And if it was necessary for David to stir himself up to the praises of God, how powerful a stimulant must we require for a more difficult matter when we aim at the divine life with self-denial. As to the religious exercise here mentioned, let us feel that we will never be sufficiently active in it, unless we strenuously exact it from ourselves. As God supports and maintains his people in the world with this view, that they may employ their whole life in praising him, David very properly declares, that he will do this to the end of his course.
